sysd-q-076.title: SMS: the text message that may never arrive
sysd-q-076.text: Studies show that around 1% to 5% of text messages are lost entirely, even in normal operation. The Short Message Service, or SMS, is a mostly paid text messaging service of telephone and mobile systems that lets phones exchange short messages over cellular networks. Messages carry up to 160 characters, and the signaling protocol limits the payload to 140 bytes. Delivery is not guaranteed, and many implementations give the sender no way to learn whether a message arrived in time. Messages are treated as lower-priority traffic than voice, so some arrive long after they matter. SMS gateways let computers send messages over the Internet through a short message service center. Businesses such as banks, e-gaming, logistics and e-commerce use application-to-person messages to reach customers. The messages are not encrypted, so carriers and third parties can read them, phone-number metadata may leak, and senders can be spoofed.

sysd-q-074.title: Firebase Cloud Messaging and the registration token
sysd-q-074.text:
Firebase Cloud Messaging finds an app on a device through a token issued at first start. The client app sends its credentials to FCM, which generates a registration token, the Instance ID, for that app instance. Notifications must include it. The client passes it to the app server, which caches it. Storing each token with a timestamp and pruning stale ones keeps the set manageable.

FCM is a cross-platform Google messaging service that composes, sends, queues and routes push notifications. It superseded Google Cloud Messaging, adding iOS and web devices to Android behind a unified API. Messages are composed in the console or sent from the app server using the Firebase Admin SDK or HTTP. FCM queues messages in storage when the device is offline, as in {{ref:sysd-q-069}}, then forwards them to a platform-level transport and routes them to the target devices. In a typical design, a notification service reads events from a message queue such as Kafka, and {{ref:sysd-msg-046}} covers queues. It then dispatches requests to FCM or to Apple's service, described in {{ref:sysd-q-075}}.

sysd-q-075.title: Apple Push Notification service: reaching Apple devices
sysd-q-075.text: Apple Push Notification service, or APNs, lets third-party application developers send notification data to applications installed on Apple devices. A notification can carry badges, sounds or custom text alerts. At launch Apple stated that push notifications conserve battery better than the background processes pull technology needs, such as {{ref:sysd-msg-101}}. In December 2015 it released an HTTP/2 provider API that replaced the legacy binary interface, shut down at the end of March 2021. The maximum payload is 4 kilobytes, up from 2 kilobytes. The API uses TCP port 443, and port 2197 is allowed when firewalls block outbound access to 443.

sysd-q-006.title: Designing a notification system for Android, iOS and the web
sysd-q-006.text:
The task is to build a notification service that reaches users on Android, iOS and the web. At its center, a notification service consumes events from a message queue, such as Kafka. It forwards each request to Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) or Apple Push Notification service (APNs) according to the device platform.

A messaging solution such as FCM is cross-platform, composes, sends, queues and routes notifications reliably, and provides a unified API between app servers and client apps. When the client app first starts, it sends credentials (Sender ID, API Key, App ID) to FCM. FCM generates a registration token, also called the Instance ID, that must be included in notifications. The client sends the token to the app server, which caches it. Tokens pile up, so the recommended practice is to store each with a timestamp and remove stale ones from time to time.

For the web, the IETF Web Push protocol defines the exchange. The user agent, the client on the user's device, POSTs to the push service to subscribe. A 201 response returns the subscription URI and a push resource URI, which must be shared with the application server confidentially. The application server requests delivery by POSTing the message to the push resource. A 201 response there means the push service accepted it, not that it reached the device.

The push service stores messages for intermittently connected devices, which improves delivery reliability. The sender must give a time to live in seconds; once it elapses the service must not deliver, and it may retain a message for less time. A message can carry an urgency of very-low, low, normal or high, defaulting to normal. The device may ask to receive only messages at or above a level, which saves battery because radio use is costly. A message with a topic of at most 32 characters replaces any outstanding message with the same topic. A device that was offline then gets only the latest update.

The device acknowledges a message by an HTTP DELETE, and without one the service should retry until the advertised expiration. Delivery receipts tell the sender the outcome: 202 on acceptance, then 204 once acknowledged, or 410 Gone on failure. They matter for critical messages, since knowing a message arrived avoids retransmission, polling and state resynchronization. Transient messages, such as an incoming call, may not need reliability. A push service may expire a subscription at any time. It must answer 404 Not Found to a sender using an expired one, so servers and clients must be prepared for changes in subscription state.

Apple's HTTP/2 provider API for APNs allows payloads up to 4 kilobytes and uses TCP port 443, or port 2197 when firewalls block outbound 443. The Short Message Service (SMS) is a further channel, carried over SMS gateways through a short message service center, with messages of up to 160 characters. Delivery is not guaranteed, though, and about 1% to 5% of messages are lost even in normal operation. At scale, a push service must hold very many open TCP connections and can redistribute load with 307 redirects. Stored messages take significant storage, so it may reject large bodies with 413 but must accept bodies of 4096 bytes or less.

openers.design-a-notification-system: A notification system has to reach people on very different kinds of devices and networks. Firebase Cloud Messaging, or FCM, is a cross-platform Google messaging service that composes, sends, queues and routes push notifications between app servers and client apps. Apple's push notification service lets third-party application developers send notification data to applications installed on Apple devices, and the Short Message Service carries short text messages over cellular networks. At the center of the design sits a notification service that consumes events from a message queue, such as Kafka, and forwards each request to FCM or Apple's service according to the device platform.

reviews.design-a-notification-system: The chapter's three channels each carry their own limits. SMS reaches phones over cellular networks, but delivery is not guaranteed and about 1% to 5% of messages are lost even in normal operation. FCM queues messages when a device is offline and finds each app instance through a registration token, while Apple's service accepts payloads up to 4 kilobytes. The full design puts a notification service behind a message queue, forwards each request by device platform, prunes stale tokens, and uses time to live, topics and delivery receipts to control what a device receives.
